_ext: keys below are pipeline extensions, additive to SPEC §4
legacy_conversion_note: Original 2021 case (source/Y3/Additional/Fast Food/Case Study_ Fast Food.docx) posed an open three-way dilemma (Subway / Papa John's / Sonic) with no real figures anywhere in the source document -- Appendix B of the original is a bare list of external article titles (e.g. 'Papa John's Statistics And Revenue'), never actual numbers, so every franchise-economics figure in this conversion (start-up costs, royalty/ad-fund rates, AUV, food cost, labor cost) is a genuine externally-researched figure, not one recoverable from the source itself -- see sources[] and RESEARCH_LOG.md. Per cases/_concepts/LEGACY_DILEMMA_LOCKS_2026-08-20.md's approved 'fast-food' lock, Sonic is dropped (weaker fit for the case's walkable-suburban Meridian, ID setting, thinner public franchise-economics data) leaving a strict Subway-vs-Papa John's binary. The couple's personal financial figures (Devin's $186,000 liquid savings, $345,000 home-sale proceeds, the investor group's $275,000, totaling an $806,000 capital ceiling) are taken directly from the original source docx's Background and used as this case's own given scenario data (the same authorial latitude as any case's Background constraints) -- they are not externally sourced because they describe the fictional Reynolds couple, not a real entity. The original's annual household spending budget ($53,400) and the couple's individual incomes/student-loan balance are dropped: SPEC §1.3 forbids decorative constraints, and none of this case's deliverables need them. The original's Challenge 3 items (restaurant location within Meridian, employee count, start-up costs, annual operating costs, first-year revenue) are restructured into D1-D6 below, adding a genuine new forcing task (break-even in months, break-even monthly revenue, ROI) the original never asked for at all. During research, real published figures produced a first-year-ROI margin far outside SPEC §2's 20% cap (Papa John's dominating on ~98% relative margin using system-median AUV) -- retuned per the pipeline's own backward-loop instruction ('retune a constraint, never hide data') by modeling Papa John's first-year revenue at its own real, disclosed FDD Item 19 bottom-quartile AUV ($600K) rather than the system median ($1.1M), on the documented rationale that a brand-new Meridian, ID suburban location is more comparable to the system's lower-volume quartile than to a median pulled up by denser/urban locations -- both AUV figures used (Subway's single estimate, Papa John's bottom-quartile) are real, sourced, disclosed values, not inventions. This retuning, and the food-cost-percentage choice within each brand's real cited range, are both disclosed in modeling_assumptions/sensitivity_disclosure as the load-bearing choices responsible for the resulting 12.82% margin -- see also FACILITATOR.md.

deliverables.text: Add up the group's three funding sources to find total available capital; report the chosen franchise's fee and investment range; determine whether the top of that range fits under the group's capital, and by how much.
A first-year operating cost table: royalty fee, ad/marketing fund contribution, food cost, and labor cost, each computed as a percent of the D3 revenue figure.
Projected first-year revenue (from AUV) and net profit (revenue minus D2's percent-of-revenue costs and Appendix C's annualized fixed costs).
Break-even point in months: a one-step equation, D1's investment midpoint = average monthly net profit x months, solved for months.

Break-even monthly revenue: an equation with the unknown revenue on both sides (revenue = fixed cost + percent-of-revenue rate x revenue), solved for revenue, then compared to D3's actual projected monthly revenue.
A recommendation comparing both franchises' first-year ROI (D3 net profit / D1 investment midpoint, as a percent), informed by D4 and D5.

balance.argument_a: Subway's total initial investment midpoint ($367,940) is well over $200,000 less than Papa John's ($585,876) -- 37% less capital at risk, leaving $438,060 (54% of the group's $806,000) in reserve versus only $220,124 (27%) for Papa John's. Subway's first-year ROI (23.24%) is close behind Papa John's, so the couple gives up very little expected return for a materially safer, lower-exposure bet on a business they've never run before.
balance.argument_b: Even modeled conservatively at the bottom quartile of its own real, disclosed system performance ($600,000 AUV, not the $1.1M median), Papa John's first-year ROI (26.22%) still edges out Subway's (23.24%), and its break-even point (45.8 months) is faster despite the larger investment -- its materially larger revenue base dilutes fixed costs and a lower combined royalty/marketing burden (11% vs. Subway's 12.5%) more than compensates for the higher up-front cost.
balance.margin_basis: First-year ROI (net profit / total start-up investment midpoint) for each franchise, computed from Appendix A/B's real cited figures (see case.json.derived for the full worked figures). Papa John's B: 26.22%, Subway A: 23.24%, margin 12.82% -- within SPEC §2's 20% cap.

modeling_assumptions.text: Employees needed to open, Day 1 -- Subway: 6, Papa John's: 9 (extra 3 reflect delivery drivers). No public per-location headcount is published by either franchisor. Informational only; does not feed any dollar calculation.

Monthly fixed operating costs (rent + utilities + insurance) -- Subway: $3,500/month, Papa John's: $4,200/month. Partly sourced (Meridian's $28/sq ft/year retail lease rate [S14b] and Subway's ~1,200 sq ft typical footprint [S15]); the utilities/insurance component and Papa John's footprint are not published and are stated estimates.

Papa John's first-year revenue is modeled at its own real, disclosed FDD Item 19 bottom-quartile AUV ($600,000) rather than the system median ($1.1M), on the rationale that a brand-new Meridian, ID suburban location is more comparable to the system's lower-volume quartile than to a median pulled up by denser/urban locations. Subway has no comparable quartile data (it discloses no Item 19 data at all) so its single available estimate is used as-is.

sensitivity_note: The case's ~13% margin is real but thin, and two of its own modeling assumptions (MA2's fixed-cost estimate and MA3's AUV-quartile choice) are large enough to move it. Tier 2 Probe 5 flexes both.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: MA3 is the single most consequential modeling choice in the case. At -50% (Papa John's revenue modeled well below even its own real bottom-quartile figure) the verdict flips to Subway; at +50% (back toward the real system-median $1.1M AUV, which the case deliberately did not use) the margin blows past SPEC Section 2's 20% cap to 87.7%. The $600K base figure is itself a real, disclosed FDD Item 19 quartile figure, not invented, but the choice of which quartile represents a new Meridian location is a judgment call, stated and defended in modeling_assumptions.MA3, not hidden in a table. FACILITATOR.md's opening note and Socratic Q3 tell the guide exactly what to say if a Hero pushes on this.

MA2's Subway fixed-cost estimate ($3,500/month) is a stated assumption (Meridian lease-rate plus an unpublished utilities/insurance estimate), not a cited figure. At -50% the verdict flips to Subway (lower fixed costs help the already-thinner-margin option most); at +50% the margin exceeds the 20% cap in Papa John's favor. This is the expected shape for a fixed-cost dial that disproportionately affects the option with the smaller revenue base to dilute it against.

MA2's Papa John's fixed-cost estimate ($4,200/month) is the least-sourced half of MA2 (Papa John's footprint has no public figure, unlike Subway's). At -50% the margin exceeds the 20% cap; at +50% the verdict flips to Subway. Symmetric with subway_fixed_monthly above -- together these confirm MA2 is the case's most load-bearing assumption, as already flagged in modeling_assumptions.MA2's own Sensitivity column.

Subway's food cost (32%) was deliberately picked from the top of a real, cited 28-35% range rather than the range's midpoint, to reflect its protein/produce-based menu. At -50% (toward a pizza-like food cost Subway does not actually have) the verdict flips to Subway; at +50% the margin explodes past the cap in Papa John's favor. The direction and size of this instability is exactly what picking a non-midpoint value inside a real range should be expected to produce, and is disclosed rather than defaulted silently.

Papa John's food cost (25%) was deliberately picked from the low end of a real, cited 24-30% pizza range. At -50% the margin exceeds the cap in Papa John's favor; at +50% (toward a sandwich-shop-like food cost Papa John's does not actually have) the verdict flips to Subway. Same disclosure rationale as subway_food_pct.

P2 both-sides PASS (both sides have real numbers; Papa Johns bottom-quartile AUV choice, already disclosed in modeling_assumptions/sensitivity_disclosure, is the one real attack surface, correctly flagged rather than hidden). P3 trap-check PASS (fresh subagent independently named the identical D1-stop-early trap FACILITATOR.md describes). P4 twist-integrity PASS (independently reproduced all twist arithmetic exactly; confirmed the shared 30-to-34-percent labor twist applies consistently to both options per S11s own disclosed shared-benchmark framing, and MA1s headcount-informational-only disclaimer forecloses the one plausible unstated-convention objection). P5 sensitivity PASS (mechanical). P6 data-decay PASS after a real fix -- S11 was found to imply the cited source directly states a QSR-specific 30% labor-cost figure, when the live page only reports aggregate all-segment distribution buckets. Fixed: reworded S11 in case.md and case.json to accurately describe it as a derived estimate from the aggregate data, not a verbatim-quoted QSR figure. All other load-bearing sources (S1-S10, S13) confirmed exact; S12 has a minor characterization nuance (not blocking); S14b has trivial price drift (~$1/sqft, non-load-bearing); S15 is bot-blocked but plausibility-corroborated via search. All 6 probes recorded, 0 FAIL.

catalog.ask: Chris and Devin have saved enough to buy into exactly one franchise, and two real offers on the table -- a Subway or a Papa John's, each with a different price tag and a different profit margin. The cheaper one to buy in isn't necessarily the one that pays them back faster.
